pages.name: Opposite arrows
pages.text: Lesson 4's coil and lesson 5's capacitor, each 10 Ω at 50 Hz, now share one loop with a 2 Ω resistor on a 10 V test supply. At 25 Hz the coil's reactance halves to 5 Ω and the capacitor's doubles to 20 Ω. The current, the same through every part, lies flat. The coil's voltage peaks a quarter cycle before it and the capacitor's a quarter cycle after, half a cycle apart, so X_L points straight up and X_C straight down. R is small beside them here.

pages.name: The net reactance
pages.task: At 25 Hz the coil's reactance is 5 Ω, pointing up, and the capacitor's is 20 Ω, pointing down. What is their net reactance, X?
pages.why: Lay the arrows tip to tail: 5 Ω up, then 20 Ω down from its tip, ends 15 Ω below where it started. So X = X_L − X_C = 5 − 20 = −15 Ω, which is 15 Ω pointing down, the capacitor's way. That net arrow and R close lesson 6's triangle, so Z = √(2² + 15²) = 15.1 Ω and the current is 10 V ÷ 15.1 Ω = 0.66 A. 25 Ω adds the two as if they pointed the same way. 20.6 Ω puts them at right angles, as R and X are, but X_L and X_C lie on one line.

pages.name: Sweep the frequency
pages.text: The frequency plays from 25 Hz down to 10 Hz, up to 100 Hz and back to 50 Hz. As it rises the X_L arrow grows and the X_C arrow shrinks, so the net arrow shortens, vanishes at 50 Hz and then grows upwards. There Z falls to R alone and the dot's current peaks, at 5 A. Below 50 Hz the current leads the supply's voltage; above, it lags. Slide the frequency yourself.

pages.name: At 75 Hz
pages.task: At 75 Hz the coil's reactance is 15 Ω and the capacitor's is 6.67 Ω. How does the current sit against the supply's voltage?
pages.why: The net reactance is 15 − 6.67 = 8.33 Ω, pointing up, so the circuit acts like a resistor and a coil (lesson 6): the supply's voltage leads the current, and the current lags it. The triangle's angle is φ = 76.5°, the angle whose tangent is 8.33 ÷ 2. Leading is the capacitor's way round, true below 50 Hz. In step happens only at 50 Hz, where the net arrow vanishes.

pages.name: Where the peak sits
pages.text: The current is greatest where X_L = X_C, so the peak's frequency can be found without the slider. Set 2πfL = 1/(2πfC). Multiply both sides by f, divide both by 2πL, and take the square root: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)). With this coil and this capacitor it gives 50 Hz, where the dot's peak sits. The peak is called [[resonance]], and f₀ is the [[resonant frequency]].

pages.task: A 100 mH coil and a 10 µF capacitor are in series. Near what frequency do they resonate?
pages.why: Put L and C in henries and farads first: 100 mH is 0.1 H and 10 µF is 0.00001 F. Then L × C = 0.1 × 0.00001 = 0.000001, its square root is 0.001, and f₀ = 1/(2π × 0.001) = 159.15 Hz. 0.159 Hz comes from putting 10 µF in as 10 F. 159,000 Hz comes from leaving out the square root.

pages.name: Fifty volts on ten
pages.task: At 50 Hz the coil's meter reads 50 V and the capacitor's reads 50 V, on a 10 V supply. How can that be?
pages.answer: They are half a cycle apart, so they cancel
pages.why: The coil's voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current and the capacitor's a quarter cycle after, so they are half a cycle apart. At every instant one is as far above zero as the other is below, so together they add to nothing, and the loop still adds up: the supply's 10 V matches the resistor's. Each wave peaks at 70.7 V, which is 50 V × √2. A meter reads each part on its own, so both show 50 V. Nothing is faulty, and neither part is a supply: their voltages come from the 5 A flowing through each part's 10 Ω.

pages.name: Double the resistance
pages.task: The bench's resistance is doubled, from 2 Ω to 4 Ω. What happens to the peak?
pages.answer: It stays at 50 Hz, with 2.5 A and 25 V
pages.why: The peak sits where X_L = X_C, and R appears nowhere in f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)), so it stays at 50 Hz. There Z = R, so the current is 10 V ÷ 4 Ω = 2.5 A, half as much, and the coil reads 2.5 A × 10 Ω = 25 V. The hump is lower and broader.

pages.task: Mixed. A 6 Ω resistor, a coil of 20 Ω reactance and a capacitor of 12 Ω reactance are in series on 230 V, 50 Hz mains. What current flows?
pages.why: The net reactance is X = 20 − 12 = 8 Ω, pointing up. Z = √(6² + 8²) = 10 Ω, so I = 230 V ÷ 10 Ω = 23 A. The coil then carries 23 × 20 = 460 V and the capacitor 23 × 12 = 276 V, both above the 230 V supply. 11.0 A uses lesson 6's formula with the coil alone, Z = 20.9 Ω. 7.06 A adds the two reactances, Z = 32.6 Ω.

pages.task: Mixed. From a City & Guilds 2366 sample paper: a 40 Ω resistor, a 50 mH coil and a 60 µF capacitor are in series on 230 V, 50 Hz. What current flows?
pages.why: X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.05 = 15.71 Ω and X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × 0.00006) = 53.05 Ω, so X = 15.71 − 53.05 = −37.34 Ω, pointing down. Z = √(40² + 37.34²) = 54.72 Ω and I = 230 ÷ 54.72 = 4.20 A, leading by 43.0°. This circuit resonates near 91.9 Hz, so at 50 Hz it is below resonance: the capacitor's reactance is the larger and the current leads. 3.46 A leaves the coil out, lesson 6's formula with the capacitor alone. 3.85 A puts 60 µF in as 60 Ω.
